title: The Young Emperor Akbar Arrests the Insolent Shah Abu’l-Maali, page from a manuscript of the Akbarnama

phase.label: Lahore years: the illustrated histories, c. 1590

source.label: AIC: the Akbarnama was “Commissioned in 1589” and illustrated as Abu’l Fazl wrote it
AIC: Basawan “was particularly skilled in portraiture”

highlight.text: He was particularly skilled in portraiture and is known to have painted the faces of the young emperor and the two other figures in front of him: the regent Bairam Khan, who is standing, and the disgraced courtier Shah Abu’l-Ma’ali, who crouches in a red robe.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago
source.title: The Young Emperor Akbar Arrests the Insolent Shah Abu’l-Maali, Page from a Manuscript of the Akbarnama

source.label: AIC: a page from Akbar’s official history of his rule
AIC: “a lavishly illustrated manuscript commissioned by the Mughal emperor Akbar”
AIC record: opaque watercolor and gold on paper

work.text: Basawan, the designer of this painting, whose signature appears in the lower margin in red, was one of the studio’s leading painters.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago
source.title: The Young Emperor Akbar Arrests the Insolent Shah Abu’l-Maali, Page from a Manuscript of the Akbarnama

work.text: According to the signature, the rest of the painting was executed by Shankar, another prominent painter in Emperor Akbar’s atelier. This painting is a prime example of the collaborative nature of the art of painting in Mughal workshops.

source.author: Art Institute of Chicago
source.title: The Young Emperor Akbar Arrests the Insolent Shah Abu’l-Maali, Page from a Manuscript of the Akbarnama

moment.text: In the earlier of the manuscript pages (Figure 82), separated from the Victoria and Albert Museum volume, the concentration is on clear presentation of narrative action; [gestures] are clearly stated, and color enhances the excitement of the arrest.

moment.text: As the first opportunity for Akbar to assert his authority, this was an important event; it is illustrated in each of the two Akbar-nama manuscripts.
